title: Resolution Navigation: Context-Preserving Semantic Zoom in Typed Knowledge Interfaces
summary: This paper candidate takes as its central research question: “Does context-preserving semantic zoom improve orientation, relation comprehension, and return-path recovery in typed knowledge interfaces relative to conventional zoomable graphs and hierarchy-plus-breadcrumb baselines?” Its current claim ceiling is HCI interaction model plus formalization and bounded user-study results. The current artifact state is formal concept note; prototype-ready; explicit hypotheses and failure conditions. The next evidence obligation is compare against conventional zoomable graph, hierarchy plus breadcrumbs, and overview-detail baselines. Prior to promotion, it requires review against semantic zoom, focus+context, overview+detail, progressive disclosure, graph navigation, information visualization, hierarchical interfaces and spatial hypertext.

title: Resolution Paths as Reproducible Explanations in Interactive Knowledge Systems
summary: This paper candidate develops “Resolution Paths as Reproducible Explanations in Interactive Knowledge Systems” from material already present in the Lab corpus. Its current claim ceiling is HCI/XAI interaction hypothesis; recorded navigation path is not assumed to be a sufficient explanation. The current artifact state is explicit H4 hypothesis. The next evidence obligation is test whether shared resolution paths improve explanation reproduction, verification, transfer, and error detection. Prior to promotion, it requires review against interactive explanations, XAI interfaces, provenance trails, visual analytics history, computational notebooks, sensemaking provenance and reproducible interaction.

title: Reversible Depth: Context Recovery After Deep Navigation in Complex Information Spaces
summary: This paper candidate takes as its central research question: “Does preserving ancestry, active context, and reversible depth transitions improve recovery after deep exploration compared with conventional navigation history and breadcrumbs?” Its current claim ceiling is bounded comparative HCI result on orientation and context recovery. The current artifact state is explicit H1 hypothesis and recurring design problem. The next evidence obligation is location recovery accuracy, return time, path reconstruction, navigation errors and subjective disorientation. Prior to promotion, it requires review against navigation history, breadcrumbs, spatial memory, focus+context, overview+detail, lost-in-hyperspace literature, semantic zoom and information foraging.

title: Typed Resolution and Relation Confusion in Knowledge Graph Interfaces
summary: This paper candidate takes as its central research question: “Do relation types revealed or differentiated under focus reduce false inference compared with generic edges in complex knowledge-graph tasks?” Its current claim ceiling is empirical relation-comprehension result on specified graph tasks. The current artifact state is explicit H2 hypothesis and relation-collapse failure mode. The next evidence obligation is typed versus generic edge conditions; false-inference rate, task accuracy, response time and confidence calibration. Prior to promotion, it requires review against graph visualization, edge encoding, semantic networks, knowledge graphs, visual variables, relation comprehension and visual clutter.

title: Visible Partiality: Can Interfaces Disclose Filters and Omissions Without Destroying Usability?
summary: This paper candidate takes as its central research question: “Can an interface disclose active filters, omissions, and projection boundaries in a way that improves user calibration without imposing unacceptable workload or reducing task performance?” Its current claim ceiling is interface-transparency hypothesis and empirical HCI result. The current artifact state is explicit candidate law and documented failure mode. The next evidence obligation is measure user calibration, hidden-filter recognition, decision quality, workload, and task accuracy under disclosed versus undisclosed partiality. Prior to promotion, it requires review against filter transparency, uncertainty visualization, provenance UX, explainable interfaces, visual analytics, progressive disclosure and information scent.

title: When Is an Information Task Done? Closure Recognition in Open-Ended Exploratory Interfaces
summary: This paper candidate develops “When Is an Information Task Done? Closure Recognition in Open-Ended Exploratory Interfaces” from material already present in the Lab corpus. Its current claim ceiling is HCI task-completion and sensemaking study; no universal closure criterion. The current artifact state is documented failure mode and explicit empirical evaluation target. The next evidence obligation is measure premature stopping, unnecessary exploration, confidence calibration, answer quality and ability to identify unresolved conditions. Prior to promotion, it requires review against exploratory search, sensemaking, stopping rules, information foraging, task completion, decision support and insight-based evaluation.
